source.title: Effective connectivity reveals important roles for both the hyperdirect (fronto-subthalamic) and the indirect (fronto-striatal-pallidal) fronto-basal ganglia pathways during response inhibition
authors: Wery P. M. van den Wildenberg

confidence_rationale: Directly supports the non-collapsibility half of MECH-141: a single model containing BOTH the hyperdirect (fronto-subthalamic) and indirect (fronto-striatal) pathways best explained brain activation on stop trials, and combined connection strength was highest on successfully inhibited trials -- i.e. successful inhibition needs both pathways engaged, not one. Fast vs slow inhibitors dissociated on which fronto-caudate connection dominated. Held at 0.74 because the paper frames the second route as the INDIRECT (fronto-striatal-pallidal) pathway rather than a seconds-scale PROACTIVE one; the 'both are needed' and 'fast/slow dissociation' evidence maps well, but the specific proactive-vs-reactive timescale labels are the anchor paper's, not this one's.
failure_signatures: The complementary pathway here is the classic INDIRECT (fronto-striatal-pallidal) route, characterised within reactive stopping, not an explicitly anticipatory seconds-scale proactive route; the mapping to MECH-141's 'slow proactive' pathway is therefore by analogy (both are the longer, caudate-routed pathway) rather than a direct measurement of proactive control.

All connectivity is measured on stop-signal trials within a single reactive task; a model where one pathway sufficed on some trials would not obviously be excluded by the group-level 'both pathways' winning model.

mapping.source_claim_statement: During response inhibition, a right-lateralized model containing BOTH the hyperdirect (rIFG/preSMA->STN) and indirect (cortex->caudate) fronto-basal-ganglia pathways best explains stop-trial activation, with combined connection strength highest on successful stops; fast inhibitors show stronger rIFG->caudate connectivity, slow inhibitors stronger preSMA->caudate.
mapping.ree_translation: Supports MECH-141's requirement that arbitration include BOTH a fast fronto-subthalamic route and a longer caudate-routed route -- and that they act together rather than being substitutable -- which is the substance of 'cannot be collapsed into a single arbitration signal'. The fast/slow-inhibitor dissociation on caudate connectivity is evidence that the longer pathway carries distinct control regimes.
mapping.mapping_caveat: The longer pathway here is the anatomical INDIRECT pathway characterised during reactive stopping, not an explicitly proactive/anticipatory seconds-scale process. Its identification with MECH-141's proactive pathway rests on both being the longer, caudate-involving route (as the Zhang & Iwaki anchor makes explicit), so this entry evidences 'two jointly-required pathways' more strongly than it evidences the specific proactive-timescale label.
mapping.source_context: Human fMRI, Simon interference task with occasional stop signals, 20 healthy adults; effective connectivity via a quantified model-comparison method (Ancestral Graph / structural-equation style).

confidence_components.notes: Source quality high: J Neurosci, careful effective-connectivity method, behaviourally-linked individual differences. Mapping fidelity moderate-good: strong on 'both pathways jointly required' and the fast/slow dissociation, weaker on the proactive-timescale identification. Transfer risk moderate: healthy human data on a well-validated inhibition task.
